analysis.one_liner: Closes a Clean Air Act loophole so toxic emissions from oil and gas wells and pipelines can be regulated together.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with 23 Democratic cosponsors, sits in the House Energy and Commerce Committee with no action scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: Current law lets oil and gas wells, pipeline compressors, and pump stations count their toxic air emissions one small site at a time, keeping each one under the threshold for strict federal pollution controls. The CLOSE Act would repeal that carve-out so emissions from these facilities can be added together and regulated as a major source of toxic air pollution. It would also require the EPA to list hydrogen sulfide — a gas common around oil and gas operations — as a hazardous air pollutant and write emission standards for it, including for oil and gas wells.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live, work, or go to school near oil and gas wells, pipeline compressors, and pump stations. These are often rural communities and neighborhoods near drilling and infrastructure that today absorb emissions of toxic pollutants like hydrogen sulfide because each individual site is counted separately and escapes federal 'major source' controls.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities near oil and gas wells and pipelines

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Clean Air Act provision that exempts oil and gas exploration and production wells, pipeline compressors, and pump stations from having their emissions aggregated with other similar sources for regulation as a major source of hazardous air pollutants.
Requires the EPA to add hydrogen sulfide to the official list of hazardous air pollutants within 180 days of enactment, making it subject to federal toxic-emission standards.

Requires the EPA, within a year of that listing, to set source categories and emission standards for hydrogen sulfide, expressly including oil and gas wells, and allows well emissions to be regulated as an area source.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators, which would face new federal permitting requirements and emission-control costs once their combined emissions are counted together, with some of those costs potentially passed through to energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators

drawbacks.text: The rules are real compliance burdens: once emissions from many wells and compressor stations are added together, facilities that individually fell below the 'major source' threshold would cross it and face stricter federal controls, and hydrogen sulfide standards would impose new equipment and monitoring costs on oil and gas operators.

Some of those costs are likely to be passed on through oil, gas, and pipeline charges, and smaller operators with scattered low-emitting wells could face disproportionate paperwork and permitting costs even where their local air impact is modest.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit runs to the people breathing air near drilling and pipeline infrastructure, who get federal emission standards for toxic pollutants that are currently counted site-by-site to escape control. The cost falls on oil and gas operators and, in part, energy consumers. The trade-off is a familiar one in air regulation: stricter control of toxic emissions in exchange for higher compliance costs concentrated on one industry. The bill gives the EPA firm deadlines, which limits the chance that the standards are written loosely or delayed indefinitely.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it now waits with no hearing, markup, or floor vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Rep. Yvette Clarke introduced the CLOSE Act on November 18, 2025, joined by 23 Democratic cosponsors.
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, and no further action has been taken since.

The bill would repeal the Clean Air Act exemption that keeps oil and gas well and pipeline emissions from being aggregated and regulated as major sources of toxic air pollution, and would require EPA to list and set standards for hydrogen sulfide.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas producers and pipeline operators, who for now face no new federal aggregation rules or hydrogen sulfide standards, while people living near wells and pipelines get no added protection.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas operators, for now

for.name: Rep. Yvette D. Clarke
for.what_they_did: Introduced the CLOSE Act to repeal the oil and gas emissions aggregation exemption and require hydrogen sulfide regulation.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of referral, controlled by the House Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has taken no action — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 23 cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill now sits in a committee led by the Republican House majority, with no Republican support on record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and well operators
industries.note: Their wells would lose the aggregation exemption that keeps scattered, individually small emission sources below the federal 'major source' threshold, and they would face new hydrogen sulfide emission standards. The cost is compliance and permitting; the public stake is air quality near drilling sites.

Compressor and pump station emissions could be aggregated with nearby well emissions for regulation as major sources, exposing midstream infrastructure to stricter toxic-air controls than current law applies.

analysis.trajectory: With all-Democratic sponsorship and a Republican-controlled Energy and Commerce Committee, the bill is unlikely to get a markup or floor vote this Congress. Comparable oil and gas emissions bills introduced by minority-party members typically die in committee without a hearing.
